newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AWF first 97/8 Australia wheat f'cast 17.81 mln/t.
newsitem.headline: AWF first 97/8 Australia wheat f'cast 17.81 mln/t.

text.p: Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd (AWF) has put the 1997/98 Australian wheat crop at 17.81 million tonnes in its first forecast.
Brian Bailey, managing director of the private forecaster, said the forecast would change many times as the 1997 wheat growing season unfolds.
AWF also said its estimate for the current 1996/97 Australian wheat crop, harvested five months ago, was 22.34 million tonnes.
This is slightly down on the Australian Wheat Board figure of 23.0 million tonnes but slightly up on AWF's last forecast of 21.37 million tonnes, issued in December.
The amount of wheat which growers would sow over the next three months was relied heavily on sufficient rain to work the soils, AWF said in its latest forecast, released on Monday.
"However, with the required rain, we forecast a wheat area very similar to that which was sown last year," it said.
The 1997 sown area would consist of more paddocks sown to wheat in Queensland and New South Wales (NSW), and less in the southern states, it said.
Pre-sowing conditions in Queensland and northern NSW are excellent, and this is where Australia's best wheats are produced, it said.
"All that is needed is one general rain of 30 to 40 millimetres between now and early June and the forecast areas will be achieved," it said.
Sowing was already in progress in central Queensland, it said.
For southern Australia at least two rains of 25 mm or more were required before early July, it said.
"At this time a general rain through southern Australia would be welcome, but growers will wait a long time before switching intentions to other crops," AWF said.
Price signals were favourable for high quality, premium priced wheats of Queensland and northern NSW, it said.
Livestock alternatives to Australian wheat growing were not attractive this year, it said.
This would ensure growers support wheat, as well as striving for more canola and pulse paddocks, it said.
On the current crop, AWF said that when the Australian Bureau of Statistics assessment was released later this year for the 1996/97 crop it was expected to show a record, but below trade estimates.
"Our reasons for the relatively low estimate of the last crop stem from the low amounts of wheat that are held on farms," it said.
Farm wheat stocks at March 31 were well below normal in each of the eastern states, it said.
